notes.vocab-analogies:
≈1 question per paper — small weight, but one fixed method makes every attempt fast and reliable

"A : B :: C : ?" — find the pair whose relationship to each other matches the given pair, in the same order and the same degree. CUET's own phrasing is almost always "select the pair which carries the same relationship" — the question is naming that relationship precisely, not just finding a loosely related word.

Common relationship types

TypeExample
Synonymmeek : modest
Antonymdull : bright
Degree (mild → intense)jog : run
Manner (verb → flawed execution of it)walk : stumble
Part : wholepetal : flower
Worker : toolcarpenter : saw
Cause : effectvirus : illness
Object : functionknife : cut
Category : memberbird : sparrow
Sequence / orderMonday : Tuesday
Symbol : representsdove : peace
Material : productwood : table

Build the bridge sentence — the one method that always works

  1. Turn A : B into one precise sentence. Not "these two are related" — an exact sentence: "to jog is to run at a mild pace."
  2. Test every option in the same sentence frame. "to drizzle is to rain at a mild intensity" ✓ — the sentence still makes sense with the new pair dropped in.
  3. Match the direction. Mild→intense is not the same relationship as intense→mild — CUET plants the reversed pair as a distractor almost every time.
  4. Match the part of speech. If A and B are both adjectives, the answer pair should be too — a distractor built from a noun pair "about the same topic" is a common trap.

Real CUET analogy questions, by relationship type

Given pairTypeReal CUET answer
DULL : BRIGHTAntonymHARMONY : DISCORD
PUNGENT : PLEASANTAntonymOFFENSIVE : COURTEOUS
ATTACH : DETACHAntonymBARREN : FERTILE
REGRET : REJOICEAntonymDESPAIR : HOPE
RUN : JOGDegree, intense → mildRAIN : DRIZZLE
WALK : STUMBLEManner — flawed executionSPEAK : STAMMER
MEEK : MODESTSynonymFINALLY : EVENTUALLY

All seven are real CUET 2022–2024 questions — the source column's options always include 2–3 distractors that share the given pair's topic without sharing its exact relationship, which is the trap the bridge-sentence method is built to catch.

⚠ Common traps

  • Right relationship, wrong order — the option pair has the relationship flipped.
  • Same topic, different relationship — both pairs are about birds, but one is part:whole and the other is category:member.
  • Part-of-speech mismatch — an adjective pair answered with a noun pair that's merely on the same theme.
  • Near-miss degree — an antonym-shaped distractor sits next to the real degree pair (RAIN:DRIZZLE vs a flat antonym like RAIN:DROUGHT), and only one matches the given pair's actual intensity gap.

Worked methods

Method 1 — Turn the pair into a sentence

CARPENTER : SAW :: ?

1

Build a precise sentence linking the given pair: 'A carpenter uses a saw as his tool.'

2

Test each option in the same sentence frame: 'A surgeon uses a scalpel as his tool' ✓; 'A painter uses a gallery as his tool' ✗ (gallery isn't a tool).

3

Keep the option that fits the exact sentence, not just the same general topic.

Answer: Surgeon : Scalpel — both are worker : tool pairs.

Method 2 — Check the direction, not just the relationship

WARM : HOT :: ?

1

Identify the relationship type: degree, mild → strong.

2

Check candidate pairs for the SAME direction: 'Cool : Cold' is mild → strong (matches); 'Cold : Cool' would be strong → mild (wrong direction, reject).

Answer: Cool : Cold — same relationship type and same direction as Warm : Hot.

Method 3 — A real CUET question, worked end to end

PUNGENT : PLEASANT :: ? Options: BRIGHT:RADIANT · NATIVE:INDIGENOUS · OFFENSIVE:COURTEOUS · SUBMISSIVE:COMPLIANT

1

Name the relationship first: pungent (harsh, unpleasant to the senses) and pleasant are opposites — an antonym pair.

2

Scan the options for pairs that are ALSO opposites, not just related words: Bright:Radiant and Native:Indigenous are synonym pairs — eliminate both immediately.

3

Submissive:Compliant is also a synonym pair (both mean 'yielding') — eliminate.

4

Offensive:Courteous is the only true antonym pair left — offensive (rude, harsh) is the opposite of courteous (polite), matching pungent:pleasant exactly.

Answer: Offensive : Courteous — the only genuine antonym pair among four superficially similar options.
notes.vocab-antonyms:
1What Is an Antonym?

An antonym is a word that means the opposite of another word. Not every "opposite" works the same way, and CUET quietly tests the difference:

Antonym"opposite meaning" — but not all opposites work the same way

Gradable

Sits on a scale — room in between. Something can be "fairly" one or the other.

hot ↔ cold (warm, cool in between)

Complementary

All-or-nothing — no middle ground. Nothing is "fairly" one or the other.

alive ↔ dead (no in-between)

Relational

The same relationship, seen from two sides — reversing the roles, not the intensity.

buy ↔ sell (same trade, two sides)

You don't need to name these types on the exam, but recognising which one you're dealing with stops a specific mistake: picking a word that's merely different from the target instead of its true opposite.

The trap CUET uses constantly

A real 2023 paper asked the antonym of CEASE and offered pause, discontinue, continue, terminate. Three of those four are synonyms of cease, planted deliberately — only "continue" is the true opposite. CUET's antonym questions are as much a test of "can you resist a synonym in disguise" as they are of vocabulary.

2The Six Major Question Patterns

Six question formats, six real CUET papers — exact wording, options, and the correct answer highlighted. Tap a pattern to open it.

1Word alone▾

From the given options, select the word which is opposite in meaning to the given word: 'ARROGANT'

HumbleProudHaughtyInsolent

Why: 'Proud,' 'Haughty,' and 'Insolent' are all near-synonyms of 'arrogant' — planted distractors. Only 'Humble' is the true opposite.

CUET English 2022 · 26 Aug Shift 1

2Underlined word in a sentence▾

Choose the correct word that is an antonym of the underlined word: "Though aware of his crimes, he remained impenitent throughout."

RepentantSmilingCheerfulSweet

Why: 'Impenitent' means not feeling remorse (im- + penitent); its opposite is 'repentant.'

CUET English 2022 · 16 July Shift 1

3Word inside an RC passage▾

From a passage on species survival — "...there are no indications that Homo sapiens is [going] extinct..." Choose the word from the passage and give its antonym.

ExistenceExtantAliveExpound

Why: 'Extinct' means no longer existing; its precise antonym is 'extant' — still existing. Note the visual near-miss: extant vs extinct differ by two letters.

CUET English 2023 · 2 July Shift 3

4Match the Following▾

Match each word in List I to its antonym in List II:

List IList II
AwkwardGraceful
AmplifyDecrease
NumerousScarce
MelodiousCacophonic

Why: Awkward ↔ graceful, amplify ↔ decrease, numerous ↔ scarce, melodious ↔ cacophonic (harsh-sounding).

CUET English 2022 · 4 Aug Shift 1

5Multi-statement select (A–E)▾

Which one of the following words is opposite in meaning to ALLEVIATE — A. Exaggerate  B. Aggravate  C. Relieve  D. Lighter

A onlyC OnlyB OnlyD Only

Why: 'Alleviate' means to make suffering less severe. 'Relieve' and 'Lighter' are near-synonyms of alleviate, not opposites — only 'Aggravate' (B) is the true antonym.

CUET English 2022 · 23 Aug Shift 1

6Antonym-pair identification▾

Which of the following pair of words is Antonyms in their mutual relationship?

Obsolete – ModernObstinate – StubbornObstruct – PreventObvious – Evident

Why: 'Obsolete' (outdated) and 'Modern' (current) are opposites — the other three pairs are synonym pairs planted as decoys.

CUET English 2022 · 16 July Shift 1

3The 5-Step Antonym Method

Use this sequence on every "word alone" or "underlined word" antonym question, in order. Step 4 is the one that's specific to antonyms — and the one that costs the most marks when skipped.

1

Recall the opposite first

Before you even glance at the options — picture the true opposite of the target word in your own head, not just its meaning.

2

Check for a context clue

If the word sits in a sentence, does the surrounding tone tell you the blank should feel positive or negative? Eliminate options with the wrong charge.

3

Decode the word if unfamiliar

Break it into prefix / root / suffix (Section 4) — negation prefixes (in-, im-, un-, dis-) are especially common in antonym targets.

4

Eliminate synonyms disguised as options

CUET routinely fills 2–3 of the 4 options with words that mean roughly the same as the target — not its opposite. If an option feels like a good synonym, that's usually a sign it's wrong for an antonym question.

5

Confirm by substitution

Mentally swap your final choice into the sentence in place of the target's meaning. If the sense flips cleanly to the opposite, you're done.

Worked example — all 5 steps, live

CUET 2023: "Choose the correct ANTONYM of the word 'CEASE'" — Options: pause, discontinue, continue, terminate.

1

Recall

Cease means to stop — the true opposite is something like “continue” or “keep going.”

2

Context clue

No sentence is given, so move straight to elimination.

3

Root check

"Cease" has no unusual root here — it's a common word, so decoding isn't needed.

4

Eliminate

Pause, discontinue, and terminate all mean roughly the same as "stop" — they're synonyms of cease, not opposites. Only continue reverses the meaning.

5

Confirm

"The meeting will continue" is the clean opposite of "the meeting will cease" — that's the answer.

Answer: Continue.

4How to Solve When You Don't Know the Word

A large share of unfamiliar antonym targets on CUET are themselves built from a negation prefix — which is good news once you know to look for it, since the "opposite" is often hiding inside the word's own structure.

1

Break the word into parts

CUET-level antonym targets are built from the same small set of Latin/Greek prefixes, roots and suffixes as synonym targets. Learn the table below once.

2

Look for a negation prefix first

in-, im-, un-, dis-, non- directly reverse a root's meaning — impenitent = not penitent, unscrupulous = not scrupulous. If the target already carries one of these, its antonym is often close to the bare root's own sense.

3

Read the sentence for tone, not detail

You rarely need the whole sentence — only whether the blank should feel positive/negative, big/small, fast/slow. That alone eliminates half the options.

4

Eliminate before you commit

Kill options that are synonyms of the target, or from a completely unrelated field of meaning, even with zero certainty about the right answer.

Word partMeaningCUET-style examples
in- / im- / un- / dis-not (negation)impenitent, unscrupulous, discontent — antonym is often close to the bare root
bene-goodbenevolent (opposite: malevolent)
mal-badmalevolent (opposite: benevolent)
-phil-love / fondnessphilanthropic (opposite: misanthropic)
circum-aroundcircumspect (opposite: reckless — no direct prefix-swap here)
-loqu- / -log-speakloquacious (opposite: taciturn)
pugna-fightpugnacious (opposite: amiable)
-vol-willmalevolent (opposite: benevolent)
-cred-believecredulous (opposite: sceptical)

Worked example — root-word decoding

Choose the antonym of IMPENITENT.

1

Break the word

im- (not) + penitent (feeling regret, as in “penitence”) → literally “not feeling regret.”

2

Infer the sense

Since the target is already a negation, its antonym points back toward the bare root's own meaning: showing regret, remorseful.

3

Match & reject

Match to the option closest to “repentant/remorseful”; reject options that are just pleasant-sounding but unrelated (smiling, cheerful, sweet).

Answer: Repentant — the negation prefix "im-" was reversed, not a whole new word.

5The Synonym Trap & Other Antonym Pitfalls

The single biggest reason students lose marks on antonym questions they "know" isn't a vocabulary gap — it's reading fast enough to grab a familiar-looking option without checking whether it's actually the opposite, not just a related word.

The single biggest trap

When 2–3 of the 4 options all feel like reasonable words for the target, stop — that's the signature of a synonym-disguised-as-decoy question. The right answer is usually the one option that feels like the odd one out, not the one that feels most familiar.

Choose the correct Antonym of AUDACITY

Arrogance  ·  Insolence  ·  Humility  ·  Boldness

Audacity means bold, daring confidence. Arrogance, Insolence, and Boldness are all near-synonyms of audacity — only Humility reverses the sense. Three decoys out of four options is a real CUET pattern, not an exaggeration.

Choose the correct ANTONYM of DWINDLE

Diminish  ·  Shrink  ·  Decrease  ·  Increase

Dwindle means to become gradually smaller. Diminish, Shrink, and Decrease all mean the same as dwindle — Increase is the only true opposite.

Choose the most appropriate antonym of FEUD

contention  ·  ephemeral  ·  strife  ·  reconciliation

Feud means a prolonged conflict. Contention and strife are near-synonyms of feud; ephemeral is unrelated (means short-lived); reconciliation is the genuine opposite — making peace instead of fighting.

Three checks to run whenever an antonym question feels harder than the vocabulary alone should be:

  • Synonym check — does this option mean roughly the same as the target? If yes, it's almost certainly a decoy, not the answer.
  • Negation check — does the target word already carry in-/im-/un-/dis-? Its antonym may just be the bare root's own sense.
  • Odd-one-out check — in a set of 4, does one option feel unrelated to the other three? That's often the real antonym hiding in plain sight.

notes.vocab-synonyms:
1What Is a Synonym?

A synonym is a word (or short phrase) that means the same, or nearly the same, as another word. The word "nearly" is doing real work here — true one-to-one synonyms are rare in English. Most synonym pairs share a core meaning but differ in intensity (happy → elated, same idea, much stronger), formality (house → residence, same idea, more formal), or connotation — the emotional shading a word carries beyond its dictionary meaning (thrifty feels like a compliment; stingy describes the same behaviour as a criticism).

This is exactly why CUET never asks for "the meaning" of a word — it always asks for the option "closest in meaning." That phrasing is a deliberate signal: among the four options, a perfect match usually doesn't exist. Your job is not to find a flawless synonym; it is to find the best available one and rule out the three that are worse. Once you read every synonym question this way, a whole category of "trick" options stops being tricky.

Key idea

Synonym questions test relative closeness of meaning, not exact equivalence. Rank the options in your head — don't just scan for "a word I recognise."

2The Six Major Question Patterns

Six question formats, six real CUET papers — exact wording, options, and the correct answer highlighted, so you can see the actual variety rather than a paraphrase. Tap a pattern to open it.

1Word alone▾

Choose the word from the given options that is closest in meaning to the given word: 'PUGNACIOUS'

RebelliousAmusingQuarrelsomeDesirable

Why: 'Pugnacious' means quick to argue or fight, matching 'quarrelsome.'

CUET English 2022 · 17 Aug Shift 1

2Underlined word in a sentence▾

Give the synonym of the underlined word: "As she grew older, she became more articulate."

athleticexpressivecunningsleepy

Why: 'Articulate' means able to express oneself clearly and fluently, matching 'expressive.'

CUET English 2022 · 20 July Shift 1

3Word inside an RC passage▾

From a passage about preparing for interviews: "Choose a word from the passage that is closest in meaning to 'Unwelcome'."

formalfrequentlyforbiddingvenue

Why: 'Forbidding' describes something unwelcoming or intimidating — the passage used it for a room's atmosphere.

CUET English 2023 · 15 June Shift 3

4Match the Following▾

Match each word in List I to its meaning in List II:

List IList II
HailGreet
JustHonest
LureAttract
RadiantGlowing

Why: Hail = greet, Just = honest/fair, Lure = attract, Radiant = glowing.

CUET English 2023 · 1 June Shift 1

5Multi-statement select (A–E)▾

Choose from the given list of words one that is nearest in meaning to IMAGINATION — A. Argue  B. Ornament  C. National  D. Fantasy  E. Mathematics

A, B, E onlyC onlyA onlyD only

Why: 'Imagination' means the ability to form new ideas or images, closest in meaning to 'fantasy' (D).

CUET English 2022 · 4 Aug Shift 1

6Synonym-pair identification▾

Which of the following pairs of words is Synonymous in their mutual relationship?

Indifferent – UncaringNimble – SlowNourish – StarveNasty – Benevolent

Why: 'Indifferent' and 'Uncaring' both describe a lack of concern; the other three pairs are antonyms planted as decoys.

CUET English 2022 · 16 July Shift 1

3The 5-Step Synonym Method

Use this sequence on every "word alone" or "underlined word" synonym question, in order. Skipping a step is where marks are lost — usually step 1.

1

Recall your own meaning first

Before you even glance at the options. Reading the options first anchors your brain to whichever one looks familiar, even when it's wrong.

2

Check for a context clue

If the word sits in a sentence, is the surrounding tone positive, negative, or neutral? Eliminate any option with the wrong emotional charge immediately.

3

Decode the word if unfamiliar

Break it into prefix / root / suffix (Section 4). A rough sense beats a blind guess.

4

Eliminate strategically

Drop opposites of the target word, words from an unrelated field of meaning, and options that are near-synonyms of each other — CUET usually rejects both when two options mean almost the same thing.

5

Confirm by substitution

Mentally drop your final choice back into the original sentence or phrase. If it reads naturally, you're done.

Worked example — all 5 steps, live

CUET 2022: "Choose the word from the given options that is closest in meaning to: 'PUGNACIOUS'" — Options: Rebellious, Amusing, Quarrelsome, Desirable.

1

Recall

Pugnacious feels aggressive — “eager to argue or fight.”

2

Context clue

No sentence is given here, so there's no tone clue to check — move straight to elimination.

3

Root check

pugna- is the Latin root for “fight” (as in pugilist, a boxer) — confirms the “aggressive/quarrelsome” sense.

4

Eliminate

Amusing and Desirable are unrelated fields of meaning — gone. Rebellious is close but describes defying authority, not picking fights — a near-miss.

5

Confirm

Quarrelsome substitutes cleanly for “pugnacious” in any sentence — that's the answer.

Answer: Quarrelsome.

4How to Solve When You Don't Know the Word

On any paper, a handful of target words will be genuinely unfamiliar. Guessing blind costs marks CUET is specifically designed to reward you for recovering. Work through these four moves, in order — most unknown-word questions fall to the first two.

1

Break the word into parts

CUET-level vocabulary is overwhelmingly built from a small set of Latin/Greek prefixes, roots and suffixes. Learn the table below once and it unlocks hundreds of words you've never seen.

2

Read the sentence for tone, not detail

You rarely need the whole sentence — only whether the word being described is good/bad, big/small, fast/slow, loud/quiet. That alone eliminates half the options.

3

Use a cognate

Many CUET-level words have a near-identical cousin in Hindi/Sanskrit-derived vocabulary (benevolent ≈ “beneficial”; malevolent ≈ “malicious”) — trust a faint family resemblance over a total guess.

4

Eliminate before you commit

Even with zero idea of the target word, you can often kill 2 of 4 options because they sit in a completely different field of meaning than the sentence suggests.

Word partMeaningCUET-style examples
bene-goodbenevolent (good-willed), benefactor, benefit
mal-badmalevolent (ill-willed), malign, malice
-phil-love / fondnessphilanthropy (love of humankind), bibliophile
-phobiafearclaustrophobia, xenophobia
circum-aroundcircumvent, circumspect, circumference
-loqu- / -log-speakeloquent, loquacious (talkative), dialogue
in- / un- / non-not (negation)inevitable, unscrupulous, nonchalant
pugna-fightpugnacious, pugilist
-vol-willbenevolent, malevolent, volatile
-cred-believecredible, incredulous

Worked example — root-word decoding

Choose the synonym of BENEVOLENT.

1

Break the word

bene- (good, as in benefit, benefactor) + -vol- (will, as in volunteer) → literally “good will.”

2

Infer the sense

That points to a meaning like kind, generous, well-meaning — you don't need to have memorised the word to get this far.

3

Match & reject

Match to the option closest to “kind/charitable”; reject options meaning “greedy” or “strict,” which sit in the opposite field.

Answer: Charitable / kind — built from “good” (bene-) + “will” (-vol-).

5Context, Tone, Formality & Collocation

Vocabulary knowledge alone doesn't clear every CUET synonym question — a large share of the "hard" ones are hard precisely because you already know the word, but the sentence is quietly narrowing which of its several senses is wanted, or is testing formality/collocation rather than raw meaning.

The single biggest trap

The most common way students lose marks on words they actually know is picking a synonym of the wrong sense of the target word. Multi-sense words are CUET's favourite trap material — always re-read the exact sentence the word sits in before choosing.

"…galvanized roof…" — closest in meaning to galvanized

heated up  ·  well lit  ·  moulded with a hammer  ·  coated

“Galvanized” has an electrical sense (energised) and a metallurgy sense (zinc-coated, to prevent rust). The passage is about a roof, so only the metallurgy sense applies — coated is correct even though “energised” is the more common everyday meaning.

"I hailed this connection with delight" — meaning of hailed

avoided  ·  refused  ·  acclaimed  ·  released

“Hail” can mean “to call out to” or “to greet/welcome enthusiastically.” The phrase “with delight” is the tone clue that selects the second, positive sense — acclaimed.

"…still in the nascent stages…" — closest to nascent

difficult  ·  matured  ·  early  ·  developed

Collocation check: “nascent stages” is a fixed academic phrase meaning “early, just beginning to develop” — recognising the phrase, not just the word, gives the answer instantly.

Three checks to run whenever a synonym question feels harder than the vocabulary alone should be:

  • Sense check — does the target word have more than one common meaning? If so, which one fits this exact sentence?
  • Register check — is the passage formal (a report, an essay) or informal (a conversation, a story)? Match the option's formality, not just its meaning.
  • Collocation check — does the target word appear as part of a fixed phrase ("nascent stages," "galvanized iron," "hailed a decision")? The phrase often carries a specific, narrower meaning than the word alone.

notes.vocab-idioms:
≈3 questions per paper — pure recall across three question shapes, so a drilled list converts directly to marks

An idiom's meaning is not the sum of its words — "once in a blue moon" has nothing to do with colour or the moon. CUET tests idioms in three distinct question shapes, and spotting which one you're facing tells you exactly what to do:

Question shapeWhat it looks like
Meaning-selectThe idiom (often underlined in a sentence) — pick its meaning from 4 options.
Complete-the-idiomA sentence with a blank inside a fixed phrase — pick the one word that completes it exactly; near-synonyms of the fixed word are wrong.
Replace-the-underlined-partA sentence with a literal phrase underlined — pick the idiom that means the same thing.

⚠ Common traps

  • The literal-meaning option is always there — reject it outright.
  • Two idioms with close meanings ('beat about the bush' vs 'sit on the fence') — match to the exact situation described, not just the general vibe.
  • 'Complete the idiom' — the fixed word is fixed; near-synonyms are wrong ('blessing in disguise', not 'in secret').
  • Match-List questions scramble idiom and meaning across two columns — solve one pair you're sure of first, it usually eliminates two options outright.

Worked methods

Method 1 — Reject the literal reading first

'After the scandal, his political career was a house of cards.' What does the idiom suggest?

1

Note the literal image: a house of cards is fragile and collapses easily.

2

Reject any option describing an actual house or actual cards — that's the literal-reading trap.

3

Map the fragility image onto the sentence's subject: his career.

4

Choose the option describing something unstable, likely to collapse.

Answer: His career was fragile/unstable and likely to collapse — not literally about a house or cards.

Method 2 — Complete the fixed phrase

'It only happens once in a ____ moon.' Choose the correct word.

1

Recognise this as a fixed idiom, not a free choice of adjective — the wording is set.

2

Recall the idiom exactly: 'once in a blue moon' = very rarely.

3

Reject near-sounding but wrong words (full, new, half) — idioms don't accept synonyms for their fixed word.

Answer: Blue — the idiom is fixed as 'once in a blue moon'.

Method 3 — Replace a literal phrase with the matching idiom

Rewrite so the underlined part becomes an idiom: 'He ignored it deliberately when his friend cheated.'

1

Identify the plain-English action being described: choosing not to notice something on purpose.

2

Recall the idiom that means exactly that: 'to turn a blind eye (to something)'.

3

Check it slots back into the sentence naturally: 'He turned a blind eye when his friend cheated.'

Answer: Turned a blind eye — the idiom for deliberately ignoring something.

adverse / averseadverse = unfavourable (conditions); averse = opposed (to)
assured / insured / ensuredassured = told confidently; insured = covered by a policy; ensured = made certain
sore / soarsore = painful; soar = fly high
discreet / discretediscreet = tactful/careful; discrete = separate, distinct
envelop / envelopeenvelOp (verb) = surround; envelOPE (noun) = the paper mailer
lay / lielay = to place something (takes an object); lie = to recline (no object)
farther / furtherfarther = physical distance; further = figurative/additional
fewer / lessfewer = countable nouns; less = uncountable nouns
its / it'sits = possessive; it's = it is / it has
comprehensible / comprehensivecomprehensible = able to be understood; comprehensive = complete, covering everything

Pattern 1 method

  1. Read the whole sentence, not just around the blank — the earlier clause sets the register.
  2. Try each option aloud in the sentence; the wrong ones usually break a collocation ("do a mistake" ✗, "make a mistake" ✓).
  3. For a homonym pair, decide by meaning first, sound second — two words that sound identical (sore/soar, flour/flower) can never both be right.

Pattern 2 — One-word substitution: CUET's own glossary

The other half of Word Usage is a vocabulary of single words that replace a whole phrase — usually Latin- or Greek-rooted. CUET reuses a fairly fixed pool; these are all real correct answers from 2022–2025 papers.

Definition givenAnswer
Something that has no beginning or end and exists foreverEternal
An act of speaking to one's own selfSoliloquy
A large enclosed area where birds are keptAviary
A book published yearly with the calendar and religious datesAlmanac
One who is new and inexperienced in a jobNovice
One who hates mankindMisanthrope
Recurring every ten yearsDecennial
Fear of waterHydrophobia
Period of ten yearsDecade
One who loves and collects booksBibliophile
The killing of a new-born childInfanticide
One who abstains from alcoholic drinkTeetotaller
A person who spends money recklesslySpendthrift / Extravagant
A person who helps a stranger in troubleSamaritan
Inhabitant of a cityCitizen
Someone who does skilled work with their handsArtisan
To understandApprehension (verb: apprehend) — not Comprehension, a planted near-twin

Pattern 2 method

  1. Strip the definition to its single core idea before scanning options — "keeps birds" not "large enclosed area for birds".
  2. Recall the term directly if you know it; if not, listen for a root you recognise (-phobia = fear, -cide = killing, bibli- = book, mis-anthrope = hater of people).
  3. Eliminate options that are a near-twin word with a different meaning — CUET's classic substitution trap is apprehension (understanding/fear) vs comprehension (understanding) planted side by side.

⚠ Common traps

  • Meaning fits but the collocation doesn't — 'heavy rain' ✓, 'strong rain' ✗.
  • Register clash — a chatty word in a formal sentence.
  • One-word substitution near-twins — apprehension/comprehension, illicit/elicit, affect/effect placed as sibling options to test if you actually know the word or just recognise its shape.
  • Two homonym options are both real words (chilli/chilly, flour/flower) — only one fits the sentence's actual meaning.

Worked methods

Method 1 — Read the whole sentence for register

'The committee will ____ a decision after the review.' Choose: take / do / give / make.

1

Read past the blank to the end of the sentence for tone and context — formal committee language.

2

Test each option as a real collocation: 'take a decision' ✓ (also acceptable), 'do a decision' ✗, 'give a decision' ✗ (used only for judges), 'make a decision' ✓.

3

Between the two workable options, CUET typically expects the more standard textbook form.

Answer: Take (or make) — 'do a decision' and 'give a decision' break the standard collocation.

Method 2 — Confusable pairs by meaning, not sound

'The scarf is a lovely ____ to the coat.' Choose: complement / compliment.

1

Don't be misled by the similar sound — decide by meaning.

2

'Complement' = completes or goes well with; 'compliment' = an expression of praise.

3

The scarf is completing/matching the coat, not praising it.

Answer: Complement — the scarf completes the outfit.

Method 3 — Decode a one-word-substitution definition

'One who hates mankind.' Choose: Sadist / Narcissist / Misanthrope / Misologist — a real 2025 CUET question.

1

Break the definition into its core idea: a person who hates people in general.

2

Recognise the root '-anthrope' (Greek for human being) inside 'misanthrope' — mis- (hate) + anthrope (mankind).

3

Eliminate the near-twins: a sadist enjoys causing pain (not the same as hating mankind), a narcissist loves themselves, a misologist hates reasoning/argument, not people.

Answer: Misanthrope — the only option built from roots that literally mean 'hater of mankind'.
notes.vocab-spelling:
Under 1 question per paper — but pure recall across three question shapes, so one pass banks free marks

"Spelling" is actually three different instructions in CUET, and misreading which one you got costs marks even when you know every word on the page:

InstructionWhat to do
Choose the correctly spelt wordPick the one option that's right — the other 3 are near-miss typos.
Choose the misspelt wordCUET occasionally flips the instruction — read it twice. Here the three CORRECT spellings are distractors and the WRONG one is the answer.
Homophone fill-blankTwo blanks, two words that sound identical but mean and spell differently (flour/flower, chilli/chilly, peal/peel).

Watch-list (correct spellings)



All 32 of these are real correct answers from 2022–2025 CUET papers — the full, filterable list is in the Spelling Bank below.

Rules that help

  • i before e except after c (receive, deceive) — with known exceptions (seize, weird).
  • Double the final consonant before -ing/-ed when a short stressed vowel precedes it (begin → beginning, refer → referred).
  • -able vs -ible: -able if a full word remains (accept → acceptable); often -ible if not (visible, terrible).
  • Silent letters recur in the same handful of words — the b in subtle/doubt, the p in psychology/pneumonia, the gh in through.
  • British spelling throughout: -ise not -ize (organise), -our not -or (colour, favour), doubled l before a suffix (travelled, cancelled).

The Spelling Bank

63 words · 33 real-PYQ-tested — searchable, opens in a full-screen window

⚠ Common traps

  • Single/double letters — accommodate (2 c, 2 m), necessary (1 c, 2 s).
  • British vs American forms are both "correct" — CUET follows British (colour, favour, travelled).
  • The inverted instruction — a real 2023 question asked for the MISSPELT word among Botanist/Entomelogist/Zoologist/Astronomer; the answer was the fake spelling 'Entomelogist' itself (correct: Entomologist), not the profession you don't recognise.
  • Homophones that are both real words — chilli/chilly, flour/flower, discreet/discrete, career/carrier — only sentence meaning decides, spelling instinct alone won't.

Worked methods

Method 1 — Break the word into sound-parts

Which is correct: acommodation / accommodation / accomodation?

1

Say the word in syllable chunks: ac-com-mo-da-tion.

2

Recall the rule of thumb for this word specifically: double c AND double m (a commonly tested exception).

3

Check each option against that: 'acommodation' is missing a c; 'accomodation' is missing an m.

Answer: Accommodation — double c, double m.

Method 2 — Use a known rule

Which is correct: recieve / receive?

1

Apply 'i before e, except after c'.

2

The word has a 'c' right before the ie/ei — so it takes 'ei', not 'ie'.

Answer: Receive — 'e' before 'i' after 'c'.

Method 3 — The inverted instruction (find the MISSPELT word)

Choose the MISSPELT word: Botanist / Entomelogist / Zoologist / Astronomer — a real CUET question.

1

Read the instruction carefully first — this one asks for the WRONG spelling, not the right one.

2

Check each word against its known-correct form: Botanist ✓, Zoologist ✓, Astronomer ✓ — all standard.

3

'Entomelogist' breaks the pattern of the others (-ologist, not -elogist) — the correct spelling is Entomologist.

Answer: Entomelogist — it's the fake spelling; the real word is Entomologist.
notes.vocab-foreign-words:
Under 1 question per paper — a fixed, learnable list. CUET asks for the meaning, occasionally as a List I/List II match.

Latin, French and other borrowed expressions used in formal written English. Learn opposite pairs together — CUET likes planting both halves of a pair as sibling options.

High-frequency foreign expressions

ExpressionMeaning
bona fidegenuine, in good faith
status quothe existing state of affairs
vice versathe other way round
per sein itself

carte blanchefull freedom to act
fait accomplia thing already done, past arguing
prima facieon first impression / at first sight
de factoin practice, whether by right or not
de jureby legal right (opposite of de facto)
quid pro quosomething given for something received
bourgeoismiddle-class (often mildly critical)
rendezvousa meeting at an agreed time and place
nom de plumea writer's pen-name

au revoiruntil we meet again

Real CUET foreign-word questions

Word / expressionReal CUET answer
MAESTROMaster
GRATISFree of charge
DENOUEMENTThe conclusion of a play
NEXUSConnection
LITERATILiterary persons
LACUNAShortcoming / gap
VERSUSAgainst

⚠ Common traps

  • de facto (in practice) vs de jure (by law) — opposites, often both in the options.
  • prima facie means "on the face of it", not "most important" or "proven beyond doubt".
  • CUET sometimes misspells its own distractor — a real question offered 'Prima Face' next to the correct 'Prima Facie'; read the Latin spelling as carefully as the meaning.
  • Match-List questions pair the foreign word in List I with its meaning in List II — solve the one you're certain of first to eliminate two wrong combinations at once.

Worked methods

Method 1 — Learn opposite pairs together

'The council's ____ leader had no formal title, but everyone obeyed her.' Choose: de facto / de jure.

1

Recall the pair: de facto = in practice; de jure = by law.

2

The sentence says she had 'no formal title' (not legal) but people still obeyed her (in practice).

Answer: De facto — she led in practice, without legal/official standing.

Method 2 — Match to the nearest English sense

Choose the meaning of PRIMA FACIE.

1

Recall the literal Latin: 'at first face/appearance.'

2

Map it to the closest English idiom: 'at first sight' or 'on the face of it.'

3

Reject options implying certainty ('proven beyond doubt') — prima facie is about a first impression, not final proof.

Answer: On first impression / at first sight.

Method 3 — A real CUET question

Which expression means the same as DENOUEMENT?

1

Recall the French root: dénouement literally means 'the untying' (of a knot).

2

Map that to its use in English: the resolution/conclusion of a story or play, where the plot's threads are untied.

3

Reject options describing other story elements (a political representation, an accomplished fact, a tragedy) — none describe an ending specifically.

Answer: The conclusion of a play — denouement is specifically the final resolution.
notes.vocab-phrasal-verbs:
≈1–2 questions per paper — often as a List I/List II match, so learn these in verb-families, not one at a time

Verb + particle (preposition/adverb) with a meaning you can't always predict from the parts: put off = postpone, call off = cancel, carry out = perform. CUET asks for the meaning, for the right particle to complete a sentence, or — most often in recent papers — as a 4-way List I/List II match.

Frequently tested, grouped by base verb

Base verbPhrasal forms and meanings
CALLcall off = cancel · call on = visit · call for = demand/require · call out = challenge publicly
BREAKbreak down = stop working / lose emotional control · break into = enter by force · break out = start suddenly (fire, disease) · break up = end a relationship
GIVEgive up = quit · give in = surrender · give away = donate or reveal · give out = distribute or run out
LOOKlook into = investigate · look up to = admire · look out for = watch for · look up = search for information
BRINGbring up = raise (a child / a topic) · bring about = cause to happen · bring out = launch, publish
PUTput off = postpone · put up with = tolerate · put on = wear · put down = write, or belittle
COMEcome across = find by chance · come about = happen · come over = visit, or affect suddenly · come by = obtain
CARRYcarry out = perform, execute · carry on = continue · carry off = achieve successfully
TAKEtake off = remove, or (a plane) depart · take up = start a hobby · take after = resemble a relative · take over = assume control

The particle itself often carries a pattern

ParticleRecurring sense
upcompletion or increase — clean up, speak up, use up
downreduction, failure or stopping — break down, calm down, turn down
offcancellation, separation or departure — call off, set off, cut off
outdiscovery, completion or exhaustion — find out, run out, carry out
intoinvestigation or collision — look into, run into, break into
on / uponcontinuation or dependence — carry on, count on, depend on

Method

  1. Read the whole sentence — the object tells you the sense ("bring up a child" vs "bring up an issue").
  2. For a Match-List question, solve the pair you're certain of first — with only 4 options, one confirmed pair usually eliminates two of the four combinations outright.
  3. If choosing a particle, test each: only one makes idiomatic sense in context, not just grammatical sense.

⚠ Common traps

  • Same verb, different particle, very different meaning — give in ≠ give up ≠ give away.
  • Picking the literal preposition ("look at the problem") when the idiom needs "look into".
  • A real 2023 question tested 'bear down / bear up / bear out / bear with' as four DIFFERENT meanings for one blank — treat each particle as a separate verb, never interchangeable.
  • Match-List distractors often swap two correct pairs' particles — 'call off = visit' (wrong; that's call on) is a genuine planted trap, not a typo.

Worked methods

Method 1 — Let the object decide the sense

'She was ____ by her grandparents in a small village.' Choose: brought up / brought about.

1

Look at the object: 'by her grandparents' signals upbringing/raising, not causing an event.

2

'Bring up' (a child) = raise; 'bring about' = cause to happen — only one fits a person as the object here.

Answer: Brought up — raised by her grandparents.

Method 2 — Don't confuse near-identical particles

'He always ____ his commitments.' Choose: gives up / gives in / gives away.

1

List the three meanings: give up = quit; give in = surrender; give away = donate or reveal.

2

The sentence clearly needs 'abandon' — check which phrasal verb matches that sense exactly.

Answer: Gives up — abandons his commitments.

Method 3 — A real CUET Match-List question

Match: Call off / Look up to / Run into / Turn up — with: To respect or admire · To arrive or appear · To cancel or stop · To meet by chance.

1

Solve the one you're most certain of first: 'call off' unmistakably means to cancel — pair it with 'To cancel or stop something'.

2

That single confirmed pair already removes 2 of the 4 answer-combination options that paired 'call off' differently.

3

Work the remaining three the same way: look up to = admire, run into = meet by chance, turn up = arrive.

Answer: Call off → cancel · Look up to → admire · Run into → meet by chance · Turn up → arrive.
notes.vocab-rearranging:
≈5–6 questions per paper — almost always tagged Medium. A method beats reading speed here.

Para-jumbles: 4–5 fragments (P, Q, R, S, sometimes A–E) to be ordered into one coherent sentence or short paragraph. The answer is one of four given sequences, so you can also work backwards from the options.

The method

  1. Find the opener. It introduces the subject in full (a name/noun, not a pronoun), and doesn't start with and, but, so, which, this, they, it, because.
  2. Find the closer. It often carries the conclusion — therefore, finally, as a result — or completes an idea.
  3. Chain the middle using links: a pronoun points back to its noun; this / such / these points back to an idea; however / for example / then signals what comes before.
  4. Check against the options — usually only one sequence has your opener first; verify the whole thing reads smoothly.

Linking-word cheat-sheet — what each connector tells you

FunctionSignal wordsWhat it means for ordering
Additionalso, moreover, furthermore, in additionThis fragment continues the SAME idea as the one before it — never an opener.
Contrasthowever, but, yet, although, on the other handThis fragment pushes back against the previous one — look for the idea it's contrasting.
Cause → effecttherefore, as a result, consequently, soUsually a closer — it states a conclusion drawn from what came before.
Examplefor instance, such as, for exampleFollows the general claim it's illustrating — never comes first.
Time sequencethen, meanwhile, subsequently, after thatPlaces this fragment strictly after the event it refers to.
Reference-backthis, such, these, that, it, theyPoints to a noun/idea already introduced — can never be the opener.

Worked example

P: they also help them develop new skills   Q: extra-curricular activities give students confidence   R: that shape their future choices   S: and gain real experience

Opener Q (full subject "extra-curricular activities"). "they … them" in P needs Q first. S continues P with "and". R ("that …") modifies the skills/experience in P–S. Order: Q, P, S, R.

A real CUET question, 5 parts

A. we should think twice before we speak   B. which may never heal and so affect our relationship   C. and words once spoken can never be recalled so   D. spoken words occupy an important place in relationships as   E. sometimes our words can hurt others

Opener D — the only fragment naming the full subject ("spoken words") without a pronoun or connector needing prior context. Real CUET answer: D, E, B, C, A.

Real papers mix both 4-part (A–D) and 5-part (A–E, or P–S) formats — the method is identical either way, just one more link to chain in the 5-part version.

⚠ Common traps

  • Starting with a fragment that has an unexplained pronoun ("they", "it", "this").
  • Two fragments both look like openers — the real one names the subject; the decoy uses a synonym or pronoun.
  • Not reading the assembled sentence end-to-end before marking.
  • The last option in the raw question sometimes carries leftover instruction text stuck to it (an extraction quirk of how these papers get typeset, not a real part of the sentence) — read past it to the actual fragment.

Worked methods

Method 1 — Opener, chain, closer

P: they also help them build confidence — Q: extracurricular activities benefit students greatly — R: and gain valuable life skills — S: that will serve them throughout their lives

1

Find the opener: Q names the full subject ('extracurricular activities') with no pronoun — it must come first.

2

P starts with 'they' (referring back to activities in Q) and 'also help them' (students) — so P follows Q.

3

R continues P's list with 'and' — R follows P.

4

S starts with 'that', pointing back to the 'skills' just mentioned in R — S is last.

Answer: Q, P, R, S.

Method 2 — Use the given options to shortcut

Four sequences are offered: (a) QPRS (b) QRPS (c) PQRS (d) SQPR. You've identified Q as the opener.

1

Eliminate any option not starting with Q — this removes (c) and (d) immediately, leaving only two to check.

2

Compare the remaining two only on the order of P and R — decide using the 'and' link from Method 1.

3

Confirm by reading the full assembled sentence once before marking.

Answer: QPRS — eliminating wrong openers first cuts your checking work in half.

Method 3 — A real CUET 4-part question

A. the function of the capillaries   B. and other materials to all the cells in   C. is to take nutrients, oxygen   D. the body and to take away their waste materials

1

Find the opener: A names the full subject ('the function of the capillaries') with no pronoun.

2

C completes A's verb phrase ('the function ... is to take nutrients, oxygen') — C follows A.

3

B continues the list from C ('nutrients, oxygen, and other materials to all the cells in') — B follows C.

4

D completes the sentence with the location and second half of the purpose ('the body and to take away...') — D is last.

Answer: A, C, B, D — the real CUET answer for this question.

vocab-antonyms.q: No species lasts forever. Our species has been in existence for at least 200,000 years and is not old in evolutionary terms. Consequently, we should persists for hundreds of thousands of years yet there are no indications that Homo sapiens is in decline. However, whether we have the capacity for total destruction-though nuclear annihilation or such-remains debated. Some experts argue that humans are so numerous, widespread and suited to survive catastrophe that no event would result in extinction. A collapse of global ecosystems resulting from climate change and overpopulation has also been predicted as a cause for our extinction but, again, it is difficult to accept that such events could cause human die-off everywhere. Ultimately, it is impossible to predict what might happen in coming centuries. But, more so than any other species, humanity is able to control its evolution via the use of technology, genetic modification and the control of resources these factors make it likely that we will persist for longer than has been typical for mammal species before us. From the given options, choose the correct Antonym for 'Extinct':
vocab-antonyms.explain: 'Extinct' means no longer existing; its precise antonym is 'extant', meaning still existing.

vocab-synonyms.q: In stark contrast to where I grew up-in warm, lush green Trivandrum, Kerala, filled with rich sights, sounds and people-life at the Poles is quiet. The harshness of winter brings along with it an eerie desolation and near-total silence. Survival in this frigid, dark and windy terrain is only for the fittest. A misstep can mean anything from an icy injury to a bitter, benumbed death. But while it is tenuous, life here is also humbling-physically, mentally, and even spiritually. The experience has allowed me to witness the wonderous dualities of nature: raw, brutal and unforgiving but nurturing and awe-inspiring at the same time. As the days shorten, almost all life starts to depart seeking warmer lands. But those who stay are surrounded by glacial beauty and an otherworldly stillness that stands unmatched. In peak winter months, the sun seems to live only in memory. Its absence however, is only an illusion: shimmering displays of blue, red, yellow, green, and orange auroras shifting and snaking like billowing curtains across the pitch black sky remind me that the light shall one day return. Even the emptiness of the land is deceptive. Look closely and out waddles a flock of penguins from behind an ice shelf on the Antarctic peninsula. vocab-synonyms.q: Conducting an interview should be like painting by numbers if you are properly prepared. Consider the various aspects of the interview that benefit from early preparation. Some of these may seem obvious, but if left until the candidates are at the door, they can have a negative effect on the process. A checklist will help to make sure everything is planned and some of the less obvious considerations remembered. Frequently overlooked is the choice of venue and its layout; this can affect the atmosphere of the interview and how candidates respond. The room can feel forbidding, formal, relaxed or cosy, depending on how the furniture is arranged and how the interviewers behave towards the candidates. Interviewing can be stressful for candidates and interviewers alike, so take account of this in the timing of the interviews and briefing of the interviewers. Stress levels also influence how interviewers behave towards the candidates; developing skills in how to question and supply information to candidates will smooth the flow and help interviewers improve their performance. Of course, question technique, active listening and observation skills benefit managers in other areas of their work, too. The way in which the interview is ended also has an effect on the candidates and may well effect whether the desired candidate decides whether to accept the offer of employment or reject it. vocab-synonyms.q: She ate a few mouthfuls of food and drank a cup of milk. But she lighted no fire, and when night came, no candle, but crept with her baby to bed. What woke her? The wonder was that she had slept—she had not meant to. But she was young, very young. Perhaps the shrinking of the galvanized roof—yet hardly, since that was so usual. Something had set her heart beating wildly; but she lay quite still, only she put her arm over her baby. Then she had both round it, and she prayed, "Little baby, little baby, don't wake!" The moon's rays shone on the front of the house, and she saw one of the open cracks, quite close to where she lay, darken with a shadow. Then a protesting growl reached her; and she could fancy she heard the man turn hastily. She plainly heard the thud of something striking the dog's ribs, and the long flying strides of the animal as it howled and ran. Still watching, she saw the shadow darken every crack along the wall. She knew by the sounds that the man was trying every standpoint that might help him to see in; but how much he saw she could not tell. She thought of many things she might do to deceive him into the idea that she was not alone. But the sound of her voice would wake baby, and she dreaded that as though it were the only danger that threatened her. So she prayed "Little baby, don't wake don't cry!" vocab-synonyms.q: What is green hydrogen ? Hydrogen is a key industrial fuel that has a variety of applications including the production of ammonia (a key fertilizer), steel, refineries and electricity. However, all of the hydrogen manufactured now is the so-called 'black or brown' hydrogen produced from coal. Grey hydrogen is produced from natural gas while 'Blue' hydrogen is from fossil fuel sources where the ensuing carbon emitted is captured via carbon-capture processes. Green hydrogen is when hydrogen is produced via electrolysis, the splitting of water into hydrogen and oxygen with electricity generated from renewable energy sources such as solar or wind. This is the most environmentally sustainable way of producing hydrogen. What is National Green Hydrogen Mission ? The intent of the mission is to incentivise the commercial production of green hydrogen and make India a net exporter of the fuel. The mission has laid out a target to develop the green hydrogen production capacity of at least 5 MMT (Million Metric Tonnes) per annum. This is alongside adding renewable energy capacity of about 125 GW (gigawatt) in the country. This will entail the decarbonisation of the industrial, mobility and energy sectors; reducing dependence on imported fossil fuels and feedstock; developing indigenous manufacturing capabilities; creating employment opportunities; and developing new technologies such as efficient fuel cells. By 2030, the Centre hopes its investments will bring in investments worth Rs. 8 trillion and create over six lakh jobs. Moreover about 50 MMT per annum of CO2 emissions are expected to be averted by 2030. As per its Nationally Determined Contribution (NDC) to meeting the goals of the Paris Agreement, India has committed to reduce emissions intensity of its GDP by 45% by 2030, from 2005 levels. Several major industrial houses have announced plans to facilitate India's adoption of green hydrogen. However, they are all premised on India being able to access a reliable stream of components, upgrading the manufacturing and skill levels of its small and medium manufacturing enterprises and developing a transmission network that can supply the hydrogen produced from supply-spots to industrial centres across the country. Many advanced economies, which have also announced plans and policies to develop such an economy and given their advanced industrial infrastructure, can steal a march over India. Green hydrogen development is still in the nascent stages globally and while India can take the lead in being a major producer, provided it develops the necessary infrastructure to execute all these intermediary steps. "Green hydrogen development is still in the nascent stages globally." Choose the word which is similar in meaning to the word "NASCENT".
vocab-synonyms.explain: 'Nascent' means just beginning to develop or exist, closest in meaning to 'early' (early-stage).

vocab-synonyms.q: "This is the most powerful, meaningful work we have seen', the famous artist exclaimed to the crowd. 'This is a picture of what could have been a dystopian future. His picture tells us that we can tear it up and start afresh. Think afresh. Find new solutions. Think of extraordinary ways to make it a more beautiful world. Thank you Kabir". Principal De murmured too, 'Thank you, Kabir.' She was, however, on the microphone, and therefore the whole crowd of students followed her lead. Hundreds of young voices rang out as one. 'Thank you, Kabir.' Kabir stood there and grinned. He waved his trophy. He bowed. He did a namaste. When the applause did not die down, he even did a couple of cartwheels. vocab-synonyms.explain: 'Extraordinary' means remarkable or exceptional, directly matching the meaning of 'EXCEPTIONAL.'

vocab-synonyms.q: A GIRL'S GARDEN A NEIGHBOUR of mine in the village likes to tell how one spring When she was a girl on the farm, she did A childlike thing. One day she asked her father To give her a garden plot To plant and tend and reap herself, And he said, "Why not ?" In casting about for a corner He thought of an idle bit Or walled-off ground where a shop had stood, And he said, "Just it." And he said, "That ought to make you An ideal one-girl farm, And give you a chance to put some strength On your slim-jim arm". It was not enough of a garden, Her father said, to plough; So she had to work it all by hand, But she don't mind now. She wheeled the dung in the wheelbarrow Along a stretch of road; But she always ran away and left Her not-nice load, And hid from anyone passing. And then she begged the seed. She says she thinks she planted one Of all things but weed. A hill each of potatoes, Radishes, lettuce, peas, Tomatoes, beets, beans, pumpkins, corn. And even fruit trees. And yes, she was long mistrusted That a cider apple tree In bearing there today is hers, Or at least may be. Her crop was a miscellany When all was said and done, A little bit of everything, A great deal of none. Find the synonym from the poem which means "useless".
vocab-synonyms.explain: 'Idle' means not in use or unproductive, matching 'useless' — describing the unused corner of ground the father found for her.

vocab-synonyms.q: "Arjun, I have brought your favourite thing. It is kept inside the refrigerator." My mother brought the earthen pot out and held it before me. I counted and looked for the biggest one from the shining, rotund figures of India's most desired sweet item. "Don't eat it in one go. Here take one. Why don't you bite it and eat slowly? Why do you gulp everything down without chewing? I avoided sleeping during the day and sneaked out of my mother's room. As I saw everyone is asleep, my mind turned into the devil's workshop in search of the prized item. I ran to the kitchen and pulled at the door of the refrigerator. I ran my hand over the eatables, mindlessly changing their places and dashed the door carelessly when I could not find the soft and syrupy sponges. I left, accidently making a mess and leaving the water tap open. In the evening, when my misdeeds were discovered, a visibly livid father dragged me to the center of our drawing room. To escape the beating, I feigned weeping. Hearing my sobs, my grandparents would invariably snatch me out of my father's hands. I broke free from their arms and threw my body on the bed with a thud. I did not listen to anyone's voice and pretended to be asleep. Hands tugged me at dinner time. I refused to listen to the request of taking food. Then my parents and grandparents would coax me with various offers. My grandfather hugged me and asked, "Arjun, what will make you feel better?" "Rasgulla! Give me at least ten." Because he gulped down food without chewing
Because he sneaked out of his mother's room
vocab-synonyms.explain: The passage states his father discovered 'my misdeeds' after Arjun made a mess in the kitchen and left the water tap open while searching for rasgullas.

vocab-synonyms.q: Trees give shade for the benefit of others and while they themselves stand in the sun and endure scorching heat, they produce the fruit by which others profit. The character of good men is like that of trees. What is the use of this perishable body, if no use of it is made, for the benefit of mankind? Sandalwood—the more it is rubbed the more scent does it yield. Sugarcane-the more it is peeled and cut into pieces, the more juice does it produce. Gold—the more it is burnt, the more brightly does it shine. The men who are noble at heart do not lose these qualities even in the face of death. What does it matter whether men praise them or not? What difference does it make whether riches abide with them or not? What does it signify whether they die at this moment or whether their lives are prolonged? Whatever may happen, those who tread on the right path will not set foot in any other. Life itself is unprofitable to a man who does not live for others. Those who lay down their lives for the sake of a friend, or even for the sake of a stranger, will assuredly dwell forever in a world of bliss. vocab-synonyms.q: Ecotourism's principles clearly distinguish it from conventional mass tourism. Instead of classic tourist meccas, ecotourism seeks out remote locations with strict environmental protections and operates on a small scale. Tourists, businesses, and local residents are encouraged to minimize their impact on the environment by recycling materials, conserving energy and water, safely treating human waste and properly disposing of garbage, using alternative energy, and building in a manner that fits in with natural surroundings. The financial benefits from ecotourism are passed on to the community through conservation projects, employment, partnerships and local participation in the development and management of local resources. Synonymous with "green" tourism, ecotourism promotes cultural sensitivity and respect for traditions and customs in order to avoid the kind of exploitation that has turned tribal ceremonies into side shows and relics into souvenirs. Last but not least, ecotourism plays a political role in its support of human rights and democracy. The popularity of ecotourism is a problem in itself. The original ecotourism numbers, deeply committed to conservation and actively engaged in cultural time, were willing to rough it out and go off the beaten path; but now the so-called en masse expect the comforts of home packaged in a pretty setting. A once honored treasure, it has become a commodity and a photo opportunity. Eco-tourists consume more resources and leave a larger impact on the environment. Operators require more land to accommodate this demand. As ecotourism spreads to every corner of the earth, it could end up defeating its original purposes. ALL TOGETHER is the synonym of:
vocab-synonyms.explain: 'En masse' is a French loan phrase used in English meaning 'in a body', 'all together', or 'as a whole group'.

vocab-synonyms.q: The great Roman orator, Cicero, in his celebrated treatise on Friendship, remarks with truth that it increases happiness and diminishes misery by the doubling of our joy and the dividing of our grief. When we do well, it is delightful to have friends who are so proud of our success that they receive as much pleasure from it as we do ourselves. For the friendless man the attainment of wealth, power, and honour is of little value... Thus in every case our joys are rendered more intense and more permanent by being shared with friends. It is equally true that, as Cicero points out, friendship diminishes our misery by enabling us to share the burden of it with others... But many misfortunes which threaten us are not inevitable and in escaping such misfortunes, the advice and active assistance of our friends may be invaluable... Find out a word from the passage above which means 'INEVITABLE':
vocab-synonyms.explain: 'Inevitable' and 'unavoidable' both mean impossible to avoid, prevent, or evade.

vocab-synonyms.q: Identify the option(s) with the correct synonym of the word "MELANCHOLY":
vocab-synonyms.explain: 'Melancholy' means feeling sad, pensive, or gloomy, making both 'Dejected' and 'Depressed' accurate synonyms.

vocab-synonyms.q: We humans walk with two legs (called 'bipedal') and use two hands. The evolution of bipedalism began in our ancestors, the primates, about 4 million years ago. The primates not only gave us our blood groups, but our two feet and two hands as well. Primates exhibit characteristics that distinguish them from less evolved mammals. These include adaptations to live in trees (as monkeys do), big brains, heightened sense of vision, opposable thumbs to grasp the four fingers in each hand, and more flexibility in shoulder movements. Dr. Tetsuro Matsuzawa of the Kyoto University, Japan, writes that the shared ancestor primates moved into tree tops and developed four hands from the four legs possessed by the terrestrial ancestor. This was an adaptation to arboreal life; enabling the efficient grasping of branches and tree-trunks. Subsequently, early human ancestors left the trees to start walking long distances across the land, bipedally. Thus, we created two feet from four hands during the course of evolution from our primate ancestors. The anthropologist Carol Ward of the University of Missouri, US points out that the way we humans get around the world is different from any other animal on earth. We move around on the ground, upright on two feet, but in a unique way: with one foot after the other; holding our body fully upright in a characteristic series of motions. So, it's a big deal to figure out how and why we walk the way we do, and how our lineage really diverged so much from ape like creatures. The human brain is about three times as big as the brain of our closest living relative, the chimpanzee. Moreover, a part of our brain, called the cerebral cortex - which plays a key role in memory, attention, awareness and thought - contains twice as many cells as the same region in chimpanzees. We are, thus, smarter than apes. 'Subsequently' means the same as :
vocab-synonyms.explain: 'Subsequently' means occurring after something else in time, i.e., 'afterwards.'

vocab-synonyms.q: Off to the right we hear the distinct 'bleep-bleep' - the alarm call of the chital, or spotted deer, announcing the presence of a predator. Kuttapan and Gautam go off to investigate and we begin to drive around to intercept them on the other side of the forest. Not ten metres down the road, we hear a loud 'varoom' - the call of the tiger - and we slide to a halt on the dusty road. Walking directly towards us at a distance of 100 metres is a large male tiger. It is one of the three-year-old males known to share this territory with his brother. The tiger continued his casual stroll directly towards us. When the tiger is about 50 metres past us, our reverie is broken by a commotion in the forest across the road. Anil, our guide, whispers loudly, 'Wolves!' There, propped up like little statues in a clearing in the forest, are two Indian grey wolves. Rigid, alert, clearly in a state of alarm and agitation, they begin yelping at the tiger. The tiger spins around on the road and charges off into the forest after them. This time the tiger turns round and glowers at the wolf, probably assessing the distance between them and the speed it would take to catch the wolf. The muscles of the tiger begin to twitch and off goes the wolf into the forest again. Finally, after one more of these encounters, the tiger moves some distance away and the wolf disappears into the forest for one last time. We can only assume that the aggressive and bold behaviour of the wolf meant he was protecting some cubs and wanted to be sure the tiger was driven out of his territory. The tiger, now left in peace, continues his stroll. Find out a word from the above passage which means 'day-dreaming'.
vocab-synonyms.explain: 'Reverie' means a state of being pleasantly lost in one's thoughts, i.e., daydreaming — matching 'our reverie is broken by a commotion.'

vocab-word-usage.q: Passage: I must say that, beyond occasionally exposing me to laughter, my constitutional shyness has been of no great disadvantage to me. In fact, I can see that, on the contrary, it has been all to my advantage. My hesitancy in speech, which was once an annoyance, is now a pleasure. Its greatest pleasure has been that it has taught me the economy of words. I have naturally formed the habit of restraining my thoughts. And I can now, give myself the certificate that a thoughtless word hardly ever escapes of my tongue or pen. I do not recollect ever having had to regret anything in my speech or writing. I have thus been spared many a mishap and waste of time. Experience has taught me that silence is part of the spiritual discipline of a votary of truth. Proneness to exaggerate, to suppress or modify the truth, wittingly or unwittingly, is a natural weakness of man and silence is necessary in order to surmount it. A man of few words will rarely be thoughtless in his speech; he will measure every word. vocab-word-usage.q: In stark contrast to where I grew up-in warm, lush green Trivandrum, Kerala, filled with rich sights, sounds and people-life at the Poles is quiet. The harshness of winter brings along with it an eerie desolation and near-total silence. Survival in this frigid, dark and windy terrain is only for the fittest. A misstep can mean anything from an icy injury to a bitter, benumbed death. But while it is tenuous, life here is also humbling-physically, mentally, and even spiritually. The experience has allowed me to witness the wonderous dualities of nature: raw, brutal and unforgiving but nurturing and awe-inspiring at the same time. As the days shorten, almost all life starts to depart seeking warmer lands. But those who stay are surrounded by glacial beauty and an otherworldly stillness that stands unmatched. In peak winter months, the sun seems to live only in memory. Its absence however, is only an illusion: shimmering displays of blue, red, yellow, green, and orange auroras shifting and snaking like billowing curtains across the pitch black sky remind me that the light shall one day return. Even the emptiness of the land is deceptive. Look closely and out waddles a flock of penguins from behind an ice shelf on the Antarctic peninsula. Shimmering (IV) to rise & roll like waves Choose the correct answer from the options given below
vocab-word-usage.explain: 'Frigid' means very cold (A-III); 'tenuous' means weak and slight (B-I); 'billowing' means rising and rolling like waves (C-IV); 'shimmering' means shining with a soft, wavering light (D-II).

vocab-word-usage.q: Since the last few decades, growth in human population has increased the rate of consumption of natural resources. It has accelerated the loss of species and habitation in different parts of the world. Tropical regions which occupy only about one-fourth of the total area of the world, contain about three-fourth of the world human population. Over-exploitation of resources and deforestation have become rampant to fulfil the needs of large population. As these tropical rain forests contain 50 per cent of the species on the earth, destruction of natural habitats have proved disastrous for the entire biosphere. Natural calamities such as earthquakes, floods, volcanic eruptions, forest fires, droughts, etc. cause damage to the flora and fauna of the earth, bringing change to the biodiversity of respective affected regions. Pesticides and other pollutants such as hydrocarbons and toxic heavy metals destroy the weak and sensitive species. Species which are not the natural inhabitants of the local habitat but are introduced into the system, are called exotic species. There are many examples when a natural biotic community of the ecosystem suffered extensive damage because of the introduction of exotic species. During the last few decades, some animals like tigers, elephants, rhinoceros, crocodiles, minks and birds were hunted down mercilessly by poachers for their horn, tusks, hides, etc. It has resulted in the rendering of certain types of organisms as endangered category. Match the words in List - I with their meaning in List - II. List - I List - II

vocab-word-usage.q: Since the last few decades, growth in human population has increased the rate of consumption of natural resources. Over-exploitation of resources and deforestation have become rampant to fulfil the needs of large population. As these tropical rain forests contain 50 per cent of the species on the earth, destruction of natural habitats have proved disastrous for the entire biosphere. Natural calamities such as earthquakes, floods, volcanic eruptions, forest fires, droughts, etc. cause damage to the flora and fauna of the earth, bringing change to the biodiversity of respective affected regions. Pesticides and other pollutants such as hydrocarbons and toxic heavy metals destroy the weak and sensitive species. Species which are not the natural inhabitants of the local habitat but are introduced into the system, are called exotic species. There are many examples when a natural biotic community of the ecosystem suffered extensive damage because of the introduction of exotic species. During the last few decades, some animals like tigers, elephants, rhinoceros, crocodiles, minks and birds were hunted down mercilessly by poachers for their horn, tusks, hides, etc. It has resulted in the rendering of certain types of organisms as endangered category. vocab-word-usage.explain: 'Flora' refers to plant life and 'fauna' refers to animal life of a region.

Its descendants inherit this feature and are better able to survive as a consequence. Those longer legs have thus become an 'adaptation'. Their evolution means that this particular lineage of antelopes has adapted to its conditions, thanks to its development of this features. Over the generations, the individual components of the genetic code within a species change, or mutate. So far as we know, mutations may provide no evolutionary advantage at all. They may be disadvantageous, in which case they are weeded out via natural selection; or they may be advantageous, in which case they persist through the generations. vocab-word-usage.q: The small village of Somnathpur contains an extraordinary temple, built around AD 1268 by the Hoysalas of Karnataka-one of the most prolific temple builders. Belur and Helebidu are among their better-known works. While these suffered during the invasion of the 14th century, the Somnathpur temple stands more or less intact in near-original condition. This small temple captivates with the beauty and vitality of its detailed sculpture, covering almost every inch of the walls, pillars, and even ceilings. It has three Shikaras and stands on a star-shaped, raised platform with 24 edges. The outer walls have a profusion of detailed carvings: the entire surface run over by carved plaques of stone. There are vertical panels covered by exquisite figures of gods and goddesses, with many incarnations being depicted. There are nymphs too, some carrying an ear of maize, a symbol of plenty and prosperity. The elaborate ornamentation, very characteristic of the Hoysala sculptures, is a remarkable feature. A closer look at the series of friezes on the outer walls reveal intricately carved caparisoned elephants, charging horsemen, stylized flowers, warriors, musicians crocodiles and swans. The temple was actually commissioned by Sona Dandanayaka or Somnath (who named the village after himself), the minister of the Hoysala king, Narsimha the third. The temple was built to house three forms of Vishnu. The inner centre of the temple was the kalyanamandapa. Leading from here are three corridors, each ending in a shrine, one for each form of Vishnu-Venugopala, Janardana and Prasanna Keshava, though only two remain in their original form. Match the words in the List I with their meaning in list II List - I List - II

vocab-word-usage.explain: 'Caparison' means an ornamental covering (A-II); 'exquisite' means beautiful and delicate (B-III); 'frieze' means a broad band of decoration (C-IV); 'profusion' means abundance (D-I).

vocab-word-usage.q: When I was a small child my grandparents would take me blackberry picking. It was usually late August when the blackberries had fully ripened. Grandad would drive us in his old van. Despite not being comfortable or particularly safe, Grandad's van had a character you would not find in a sleek new car, complete with the latest innovations and a silent engine. Being seven or eight at the time, I always enjoyed a trip as we bounced along to our destination. My grandparents always chose the same spot. Wild blackberry bushes stretched along the roadside as far as the eye could see in both directions. The road overlooked a small pitch and putt course. On such sunny summer days it was always full. Golfers ambled sedately from hole to hole and the crack of metal striking ball was a constant accompaniment. Several hours of picking berries ensued. Nana warned me not to eat any until they had all been washed, but turned a knowing blind eye while I gorged anyway. I also helped myself to the occasional unripe red berry as I had a particular taste for anything bitter. The fully immature green berries proved a step too far for even my palate and were merely unpleasant. When at last we were finished the bright scenery had turned to lengthy shadows and the afternoon had elapsed into evening. Grandad hauled a big bag half full of berries back to the van. Juice bled slowly onto the ground. Nana would later make apple and blackberry tarts and fill several jars with jam. When I reached the van my stomach hurt from too much fruit. My hands stung from constant thorn pricks and were stained dark purple. I always enjoyed those days. Match List I with List II with the verbs in List I to thus meanings in List II List - I List - II
opts: amble (IV) pull or drag with effort Choose the correct answer from the options given below
vocab-word-usage.explain: 'Haul' means to pull or drag with effort (A-IV); 'elapse' means to pass by (of time) (B-I); 'gorge' means to eat greedily (C-III); 'amble' means to walk leisurely (D-II).

vocab-word-usage.q: It was raining when Rahel came back to Ayemenem. Slanting silver ropes slammed into loose earth, plowing it up like gunfire. The old house on the hill wore its steep, gabled roof pulled over its ears like a low hat. The walls, streaked with moss, had grown soft, and bulged a little with dampness that seeped up from the ground. The wild, overgrown garden was full of the whisper and scurry of small lives. In the undergrowth a rat snake rubbed itself against a glistening stone. Hopeful yellow bullfrogs cruised the scummy pond for mates. A drenched mongoose flashed across the leaf-strewn driveway. The house itself looked empty. The doors and window were locked. The front verendah bare unfurnished. But the skyblue Plymouth with chrome tailfins was still parked outside, and inside, Baby Kochamma was still alive. She was Rahel's baby grandaunt, her grandfather's younger sister. Her name was really Navomi, Navomi Ipe, but every body called her Baby. She became Baby Kochamma when she was old enough to be an aunt. Rahel hadn't come to see her, though. Neither niece nor baby grandaunt labored under any illusions on that account. Rahel had come to see her brother, Estha. They were two-egg twins. "Dizygotic" doctors called them. Born from separate but simultaneously fertilized eggs. Estha-- Esthappen-- was the older by eighteen minutes. They never did look much like each other, Estha and Rahel, and even when they were thin-armed children, flat-chasted, wormridden and Elvis presley-puffed, there was none of the usual "Who is who ?" and "Which is which?" from oversmilling relatives or the Syrian Orthodox bishops who frequently visited the Ayemenem House for donations. The confusion lay in a deeper, more secret place. What would be best describe the word 'gabled' from the passage ?
opts: a triangular canopy over a window or a door
the triangular upper part of a wall at the end of a ridged roof
vocab-word-usage.explain: 'Gabled' refers to a gable — the triangular part of a wall at the end of a ridged roof (D), or by extension a triangular canopy over an opening (B).
