vocab-word-usage.q: In 1984, the French and the British agreed that a link across the English Channel would be mutually beneficial. However, both the Governments realised that although the project would create the much needed jobs, neither country's Government could fund such a massive project. Thus, they decided to hold a contest. This contest invited companies to submit their plan to create a link across the English Channel. As part of the contest's requirements, the submitting company was to provide a plan to raise the needed funds to build the project, have the ability to operate the proposed Channel link once the project was completed, and the proposed link must be able to endure for at least 120 years. Ten proposals were submitted, including various tunnels and bridges. Some of the proposals were so outlandish in design that they were easily dismissed; others would be so expensive that they were unlikely to ever be completed. The successful proposal planned for a tunnel made up of two, parallel railway tunnels that would be dug under the English Channel. Between these two railway tunnels would run a third, smaller tunnel that would be used for maintenance, including drainage pipes, communication cables etc. After the first testrun on 10 December 1993, the Channel Tunnel officially opened on 6 may 1994. vocab-word-usage.explain: A 'shuttle' refers to a vehicle or service that travels back and forth regularly between two points.

vocab-word-usage.q: We humans walk with two legs (called 'bipedal') and use two hands. The evolution of bipedalism began in our ancestors, the primates, about 4 million years ago. The primates not only gave us our blood groups, but our two feet and two hands as well. Primates exhibit characteristics that distinguish them from less evolved mammals. These include adaptations to live in trees (as monkeys do), big brains, heightened sense of vision, opposable thumbs to grasp the four fingers in each hand, and more flexibility in shoulder movements. Dr. Tetsuro Matsuzawa of the Kyoto University, Japan, writes that the shared ancestor primates moved into tree tops and developed four hands from the four legs possessed by the terrestrial ancestor. This was an adaptation to arboreal life; enabling the efficient grasping of branches and tree-trunks. Subsequently, early human ancestors left the trees to start walking long distances across the land, bipedally. Thus, we created two feet from four hands during the course of evolution from our primate ancestors. The anthropologist Carol Ward of the University of Missouri, US points out that the way we humans get around the world is different from any other animal on earth. We move around on the ground, upright on two feet, but in a unique way: with one foot after the other; holding our body fully upright in a characteristic series of motions. So, it's a big deal to figure out how and why we walk the way we do, and how our lineage really diverged so much from ape like creatures. The human brain is about three times as big as the brain of our closest living relative, the chimpanzee. Moreover, a part of our brain, called the cerebral cortex - which plays a key role in memory, attention, awareness and thought - contains twice as many cells as the same region in chimpanzees. We are, thus, smarter than apes. The word 'arboreal' means :
vocab-word-usage.explain: 'Arboreal' means relating to or living in trees, matching the passage's description of primates' 'adaptation to arboreal life.'

vocab-word-usage.q: Unquestionably a literary life is for the most part an unhappy life; because, if you have genius, you must suffer the penalty of genius; and, if you have only talent, there are so many cares and worries incidental to the circumstances of men of letters, as to make life exceedingly miserable. Besides the pangs of composition, and the continuous disappointment which a true artist feels at his inability to reveal himself, there is the ever-recurring difficulty of gaining the public ear. Young writers are buoyed up by the hope and the belief that they have only to throw that poem at the world's feet to get back in return the laurel-crown; that they have only to push that novel into print to be acknowledged at once as a new light in literature. You can never convince a young author that the editors of magazines and the publishers of books are a practical body of men, who are by no means frantically anxious about placing the best literature before the public. Nay, that for the most part they are mere brokers who conduct their business on the hardest lines of a Profit and Loss account. But supposing your book fairly launches, its perils are only beginning. You have to run the gauntlet of the critics. A time comes in the life of every author when he regards critics as comical rather than formidable, and goes his way unheeding. But there are sensitive souls that yield under the chastisement and, perhaps after suffering much silent torture, abandon the profession of the pen for ever. Keats, perhaps, is the saddest example of a fine spirit hounded to death by savage criticism; because, whatever his biographers may aver, that furious attack of Gifford and Terry undoubtedly expedited his death. But no doubt there are hundreds who suffer keenly hostile and unscrupulous criticism, and who have to bear that suffering in silence, because it is a cardinal principle in literature that the most unwise thing in the world for an author is to take public notice of criticism in the way of defending himself. Silence is the only safeguard, as it is the only dignified protest against insult and offence. Match the words/expressions in List - I with their meanings in List - II. List - I List - II
opts: buoyed up by the hope (II) middlemen
unscrupulous (IV) pain of creativity Choose the correct answer from the options given below
vocab-word-usage.explain: 'Pangs of composition' means the pain of creativity (A-IV); 'buoyed up by the hope' means overly enthusiastic (B-I); 'mere brokers' means middlemen (C-II); 'unscrupulous' means dishonest (D-III).

vocab-foreign-words.q: Choose the correct meaning for the underlined words: The Mayor appointed an ad hoc committee to study the project.

Concerned with cleaning of Municipal Area
vocab-foreign-words.explain: 'Ad hoc' is a Latin phrase that literally means 'for this purpose' — formed or arranged for a specific, immediate purpose or case only.

vocab-foreign-words.q: Choose the correct meaning(s) for the word: "Malafide"
vocab-foreign-words.explain: 'Mala fide' is a Latin phrase meaning 'in bad faith' or 'with intent to deceive.'

vocab-foreign-words.explain: 'Rendezvous' means an appointed meeting, often used to mean a secret or prearranged meeting.

vocab-foreign-words.q: Choose the appropriate option for the underlined foreign word :- There is a prime facie evidence that he was involved in fraud.
vocab-foreign-words.explain: 'Prima facie' is a Latin legal term meaning 'based on the first impression,' i.e., evidence sufficient at first glance.

vocab-foreign-words.q: Fill in the blank by choosing the correct foreign word : - The Ruling Government wants to change the fundamental rights but conservatives want to maintain _______.
vocab-foreign-words.explain: 'Status quo' is the Latin phrase meaning 'the existing state of affairs,' matching the context of conservatives wanting to preserve things as they are.

vocab-foreign-words.q: Choose the best option for the meaning of the given foreign word/phrase BON APPETIT
vocab-foreign-words.explain: 'Bon appétit' is French for 'good appetite', a phrase said to wish someone an enjoyable meal.

vocab-foreign-words.q: Choose the best option for the given expression:- in the mean while
vocab-foreign-words.explain: 'Ad interim' is Latin for 'in the meantime/meanwhile.'

vocab-foreign-words.q: Out of the four alternatives, choose the option which best expresses the meaning of the word : "Versus"
vocab-foreign-words.explain: 'Versus' means 'against', typically used to indicate opposing sides in a contest or comparison.

vocab-foreign-words.q: Choose the correct option which best expresses the meaning of the foreign word "deja vu"

a feeling that something might happen in future
a feeling that something is happening
vocab-foreign-words.explain: 'Déjà vu' is French for 'already seen', describing the feeling that a new experience has happened before.

vocab-foreign-words.q: Replace the underlined words by a foreign expression. The Lok Sabha Speaker adjourned the Parliament Session for an indefinite period.

vocab-foreign-words.explain: 'Ab initio' is Latin for 'from the beginning'. 'Ad infinitum' means endlessly, 'a priori' means from deduction rather than experience, and 'ad hoc' means for a specific purpose only.

vocab-foreign-words.q: Choose the correct option that best expresses the meaning of the Latin phrase, 'ALTER EGO'.
vocab-foreign-words.explain: 'Alter ego' literally means 'other self' in Latin — a second identity or another side of oneself.

vocab-foreign-words.q: Choose the most appropriate meaning of the following foreign phrase: "SANG FROID"
vocab-foreign-words.explain: 'Sang froid' literally means 'cold blood' in French and refers to composure or calmness under pressure; none of the listed options precisely captures this, though the source marks 'cool look' as correct, likely as a loose approximation of 'staying cool.'

vocab-foreign-words.q: Choose from the options given below the correct meaning of the foreign word 'laissez faire'.
vocab-foreign-words.explain: 'Laissez faire' is a French phrase meaning to let people do as they choose — i.e. free from interference, especially in an economic or governmental context.

vocab-foreign-words.q: Choose the correct meaning of the foreign word "A LA CARTE", out of the options given below:
vocab-foreign-words.explain: 'À la carte' refers to food ordered as individual items from a menu rather than as part of a fixed meal, with each item priced separately.

vocab-foreign-words.q: Choose the correct option for the meaning of the foreign word - "RENDEZVOUS"
vocab-foreign-words.explain: 'Rendezvous' refers to a designated, often secret or private, meeting place, or an agreement to meet at a specific location.

vocab-rearranging.q: I had never seen a house on fire before. So, one evening when I heard fire engines with loud alarm bells rushing past my house, I quickly ran out and, a few streets away, joined a large crowed of people, but we could see the fire only from a distance because the police would not allow any one near the building on fire. What a terrible scene I saw that day. Huge flames of fire were coming out of each floor, and black and thick smoke spread all around. Every now and then tongues of fire would shoot up almost sky-high, sending huge sparks of fire all around. Three fire engines were busily engaged and the firemen in their dark uniforms were playing the hose on various parts of the building. Then the tall red ladders of the fire engine were stretched upwards and could see some firemen climbing up with hoses in their hands. On reaching almost the top of the ladder, they began to pour floods of water on the topmost part of the building. This continuous flooding brought the fire under control but the building was completely destroyed. While fire is a blessing in many ways, it can also be a great danger to human life and property. Rearrange the following sentences to recreate the sequence of events as per the passage A. The narrator ran out of the house B. The building caught fire C. Fireman climbed the ladder D. vocab-rearranging.q: It was raining when Rahel came back to Ayemenem. Slanting silver ropes slammed into loose earth, plowing it up like gunfire. The old house on the hill wore its steep, gabled roof pulled over its ears like a low hat. The walls, streaked with moss, had grown soft, and bulged a little with dampness that seeped up from the ground. The wild, overgrown garden was full of the whisper and scurry of small lives. In the undergrowth a rat snake rubbed itself against a glistening stone. Hopeful yellow bullfrogs cruised the scummy pond for mates. A drenched mongoose flashed across the leaf-strewn driveway. The house itself looked empty. The doors and window were locked. The front verendah bare unfurnished. But the skyblue Plymouth with chrome tailfins was still parked outside, and inside, Baby Kochamma was still alive. She was Rahel's baby grandaunt, her grandfather's younger sister. Her name was really Navomi, Navomi Ipe, but every body called her Baby. She became Baby Kochamma when she was old enough to be an aunt. Rahel hadn't come to see her, though. Neither niece nor baby grandaunt labored under any illusions on that account. Rahel had come to see her brother, Estha. They were two-egg twins. "Dizygotic" doctors called them. Born from separate but simultaneously fertilized eggs. Estha-- Esthappen-- was the older by eighteen minutes. They never did look much like each other, Estha and Rahel, and even when they were thin-armed children, flat-chasted, wormridden and Elvis presley-puffed, there was none of the usual "Who is who ?" and "Which is which?" from oversmilling relatives or the Syrian Orthodox bishops who frequently visited the Ayemenem House for donations. The confusion lay in a deeper, more secret place. Arrange the following sentences in order of its occurrence in the given passage :
opts: The doors and windows were locked
A rat snake rubbed itself against a glistening store
Slanting silver ropes slammed into loose earth
The wild overgrown garden was full of the whisper and scurry of small lives
vocab-rearranging.explain: In the passage's actual order: the rain is described first ('Slanting silver ropes slammed into loose earth', C), then the garden's small lives (D), then the rat snake (B), then the locked doors (A), and finally the bishops mentioned near the end (E) — matching order C, D, B, A, E.

vocab-rearranging.q: In 1984, the French and the British agreed that a link across the English Channel would be mutually beneficial. However, both the Governments realised that although the project would create the much needed jobs, neither country's Government could fund such a massive project. Thus, they decided to hold a contest. This contest invited companies to submit their plan to create a link across the English Channel. As part of the contest's requirements, the submitting company was to provide a plan to raise the needed funds to build the project, have the ability to operate the proposed Channel link once the project was completed, and the proposed link must be able to endure for at least 120 years. Ten proposals were submitted, including various tunnels and bridges. Some of the proposals were so outlandish in design that they were easily dismissed; others would be so expensive that they were unlikely to ever be completed. The successful proposal planned for a tunnel made up of two, parallel railway tunnels that would be dug under the English Channel. Between these two railway tunnels would run a third, smaller tunnel that would be used for maintenance, including drainage pipes, communication cables etc. After the first testrun on 10 December 1993, the Channel Tunnel officially opened on 6 may 1994. vocab-rearranging.explain: The passage's actual order is: governments realize neither can fund it (E), they decide to hold a contest (C), the 120-year endurance requirement is stated (B), the successful two-tunnel proposal is described (A), and the third maintenance tunnel is mentioned (D) — matching order E, C, B, A, D.

To refuse to listen to someone — e.g. “He turned a de a fear to all the warnings.”
Meeting the required standard — e.g. “His work was not quite up to the mark in the final review.”
The varying fortunes in life — e.g. “Every career has its ups and downs.”
To win easily without much effort — e.g. “They won the tournament hands down.”
Complete Guide — e.g. “All idioms from both sections listed alphabetically.”
strangers in need — e.g. “A good Samaritan stopped to help the accident victim.”
In perfect order and neatness — e.g. “She kept her desk in apple pie order at all times.”

Feeling depressed or disappointed — e.g. “She was cast down by the negative feedback on her work.”
The deciding vote when others are equal — e.g. “The chairperson used her casting vote to break the tie.”
To turn pale with fear or shock — e.g. “He changed colour when he heard the news.”
In a very happy or cheerful mood — e.g. “The team was in high spirits after their victory.”
Fashionable or popular at the present time — e.g. “Sustainable fashion is very much in vogue right now.”

vocab-analogies.q: PETAL : FLOWER ::
vocab-analogies.explain: Part : whole. A petal is part of a flower as a chapter is part of a book.

vocab-analogies.q: CARPENTER : SAW ::
vocab-analogies.explain: Worker : tool. A carpenter uses a saw as a surgeon uses a scalpel.

vocab-analogies.q: WARM : HOT ::
vocab-analogies.explain: Degree, same direction (mild → strong): warm→hot as cool→cold.

vocab-analogies.q: VIRUS : ILLNESS ::
vocab-analogies.explain: Cause : effect. A virus causes illness as a spark causes fire.

vocab-analogies.q: BIRD : SPARROW ::
vocab-analogies.explain: Category : member. A sparrow is a kind of bird as a rose is a kind of flower.

vocab-antonyms.q: Choose the antonym: FRUGAL
vocab-antonyms.explain: Frugal = sparing with money; its opposite is extravagant. 'Thrifty' is a synonym trap.

vocab-antonyms.q: Choose the antonym: TRANSPARENT
vocab-antonyms.explain: Transparent (see-through / open) ↔ opaque.

vocab-antonyms.q: Choose the antonym: HUMILITY
vocab-antonyms.explain: Humility ↔ arrogance. 'Modesty' is a synonym trap.

vocab-antonyms.q: Choose the antonym: SCARCE
vocab-antonyms.explain: Scarce ↔ abundant. 'Rare' is a synonym.

vocab-antonyms.q: Choose the antonym: FAMOUS
vocab-antonyms.explain: The opposite of famous is obscure/unknown — not the non-word 'unfamous'.

vocab-synonyms.q: Choose the synonym: OBSOLETE
vocab-synonyms.explain: Obsolete = no longer in use, outdated.

vocab-synonyms.q: Choose the synonym: CANDID
vocab-synonyms.explain: Candid = open and honest, frank.

vocab-synonyms.q: 'Her ______ remarks left no room for doubt.' Closest to LUCID:
vocab-synonyms.explain: Lucid = clearly expressed, easy to understand.

vocab-synonyms.q: Choose the synonym: TENACIOUS
vocab-synonyms.explain: Tenacious = holding firmly, persistent.

vocab-synonyms.q: Choose the synonym: BREVITY
vocab-synonyms.explain: Brevity = briefness, shortness (note: not related to 'brave').

vocab-idioms.q: 'Losing that job was a blessing in disguise.' The idiom means:
opts: Something bad that turned out to be good
vocab-idioms.explain: A blessing in disguise = a misfortune that proves beneficial.

vocab-idioms.q: 'Stop beating about the bush and tell me.' The speaker wants the listener to:
vocab-idioms.explain: Beat about the bush = avoid the main point.

vocab-idioms.q: Complete: 'It only happens once in a ______ moon.'
vocab-idioms.explain: The fixed idiom is 'once in a blue moon' = very rarely.

vocab-idioms.q: 'The new tax added fuel to the ______.'
vocab-idioms.explain: Add fuel to the fire = make a bad situation worse.

vocab-idioms.q: Which sentence uses 'turn a blind eye' correctly?
opts: The guard turned a blind eye to the latecomers
She turned a blind eye and read the sign
He turned a blind eye towards the sun
They turned a blind eye of the map
vocab-idioms.explain: Turn a blind eye (to something) = deliberately ignore it.

vocab-word-usage.q: Fill the blank: 'The new policy will ______ every department by April.'
vocab-word-usage.explain: 'Affect' is the verb 'to influence'; 'effect' as a verb means 'to bring about' and doesn't fit here.

vocab-word-usage.q: Choose the correctly used word:
opts: She gave me a genuine complement on my essay
The scarf is a nice complement to the coat
vocab-word-usage.explain: 'Complement' = completes/goes well with. 'Compliment' = praise (and its past is 'paid').

vocab-word-usage.q: Fill the blank: 'Heavy rain and ______ winds delayed the flight.'
vocab-word-usage.explain: 'Strong winds' is the standard collocation; the others don't pair naturally with 'winds' here.

vocab-word-usage.q: Which sentence uses the word incorrectly?
opts: No one was there except the guard
vocab-word-usage.explain: 'Except the offer' should be 'accept the offer' — 'accept' = receive.

vocab-word-usage.q: Fill the blank: 'The committee will ______ a decision after the review.'
vocab-word-usage.explain: 'Take a decision' / 'make a decision' are both used; here 'take a decision' is the expected CUET-style collocation, and 'do/give a decision' are wrong.

vocab-spelling.q: Choose the correctly spelt word:
vocab-spelling.explain: Accommodation — double c and double m.

vocab-spelling.q: Choose the correctly spelt word:
vocab-spelling.explain: Privilege — no 'd', ends '-lege'.

vocab-spelling.q: Choose the incorrectly spelt word:
vocab-spelling.explain: It should be 'embarrass' — double r and double s.

vocab-spelling.q: Choose the correctly spelt word:
vocab-spelling.explain: Maintenance — '-ten-' in the middle, '-ance' at the end.

vocab-spelling.q: Choose the correctly spelt word:
vocab-spelling.explain: Rhythm — 'r-h-y-t-h-m', no vowel between t and h and m.

vocab-foreign-words.q: 'The agreement was a fait accompli.' It means:
vocab-foreign-words.explain: Fait accompli = a thing already accomplished, past arguing about.

vocab-foreign-words.q: A 'bona fide' buyer is one who is:
vocab-foreign-words.explain: Bona fide = in good faith, genuine.

vocab-foreign-words.q: 'De facto' leader means the leader:
opts: In practice, whether officially or not
vocab-foreign-words.explain: De facto = in fact / in practice, as opposed to de jure (by law).

vocab-foreign-words.q: 'Prima facie' evidence is evidence that:
vocab-foreign-words.explain: Prima facie = on the face of it, at first sight.

vocab-foreign-words.q: 'Carte blanche' means:
opts: Complete freedom to act as one thinks best
vocab-foreign-words.explain: Carte blanche = unrestricted authority.

vocab-phrasal-verbs.q: 'The match was ______ because of rain.' Choose the phrasal verb meaning 'cancelled':
vocab-phrasal-verbs.explain: Call off = cancel. Call on = visit; call up = phone / summon; call for = demand.

vocab-phrasal-verbs.q: 'You must ______ your bad habits.' Meaning 'stop / abandon':
vocab-phrasal-verbs.explain: Give up = quit. Give in = surrender; give away = donate/reveal; give out = distribute/fail.

vocab-phrasal-verbs.q: 'I ______ an old friend at the station.' Meaning 'met by chance':
vocab-phrasal-verbs.explain: Run into = meet unexpectedly.

vocab-phrasal-verbs.q: 'The committee will ______ the complaint.' Meaning 'investigate':
vocab-phrasal-verbs.explain: Look into = investigate. Look up = search a reference; look after = care for; look out = be careful.

vocab-phrasal-verbs.q: 'She was ______ by her grandparents.' Meaning 'raised':
vocab-phrasal-verbs.explain: Bring up = raise a child (also raise a topic).

vocab-rearranging.q: Order the parts: (P) which soon spread across Europe (Q) Gutenberg built a printing press (R) in the fifteenth century (S) making books far cheaper
vocab-rearranging.explain: Opener Q names the subject. R fixes the time. P ('which…') modifies the press. S is the result. Q-R-P-S reads smoothly.

vocab-rearranging.q: Order the parts: (P) they were later proven right (Q) many scientists doubted the theory (R) at first (S) after decades of testing
vocab-rearranging.explain: R ('at first') + Q sets the time and the doubt; S ('after decades…') then P (the outcome). R-Q-S-P.

vocab-rearranging.q: Which fragment is the best opening sentence?
opts: The invention of the wheel transformed transport
they used it for pottery first
vocab-rearranging.explain: An opener states the subject in full and doesn't begin with 'and / which / they'.

vocab-rearranging.q: Order: (P) it can also cause landslides (Q) heavy rainfall fills reservoirs (R) but on steep slopes (S) a welcome sight in a dry year
vocab-rearranging.explain: Q (subject) + S (comment on Q) + R ('but on steep slopes') + P (the contrasting danger).

vocab-rearranging.q: In para-jumbles, the word 'this' at the start of a fragment tells you:
opts: It must be the first sentence
It refers back to an idea in an earlier fragment
vocab-rearranging.explain: 'This/such/these' point backwards, so that fragment cannot be the opener.

Vocabulary — one-page revision

The split (avg per paper)

Word Usage ≈ 5.6 · Rearranging ≈ 5.6 · Synonyms ≈ 4.4 · Antonyms ≈ 4.0 · Idioms ≈ 3.1 · Phrasal Verbs ≈ 1.7 · Analogies/Spelling/Foreign ≈ <1 each. Vocabulary is over half the paper.

Para-jumbles — the drill

  • Opener: names the subject in full; never starts with and / but / which / this / they / it.
  • Chain the middle with pronoun→noun links and this / such / however / for example / then.
  • Verify against the four given sequences; read the whole thing end-to-end.

Confusable pairs

accept/except · affect(v)/effect(n) · principal(main)/principle(rule) · stationary(still)/stationery(pens) · complement(completes)/compliment(praise) · adverse(bad)/averse(opposed) · elicit(draw out)/illicit(illegal).

Synonyms & antonyms

Fix the word's meaning and its positive/negative charge before reading options. For antonyms, strike out any option that is a synonym of the target first.

Know cold: evanescent=fleeting · ubiquitous=everywhere · candid=frank · frugal=thrifty · obsolete=outdated · lucid=clear · tenacious=persistent · verbose=wordy · brevity=shortness.

Idioms & phrasal verbs — always reject

the literal-meaning option. Learn: put off=postpone · call off=cancel · look into=investigate · put up with=tolerate · run into=meet by chance · give in≠give up≠give away.

Foreign words

bona fide=genuine · status quo=existing state · de facto=in practice / de jure=by law · prima facie=at first sight · fait accompli=already done · carte blanche=full freedom · quid pro quo=something for something.
